visuals.heading: Get the Skill Stack and the Proof

blocks.heading: Strip Away the "Media and Events" Branding

items.text: None of that is as glamorous as it sounds in a job description.
The "big win" moments - a front-page story, a trending influencer post, a well-handled crisis, happen occasionally and briefly.
Every "how to get into PR" guide eventually reduces to three real doors.
A BA in Mass Communication, Journalism, or Public Relations, followed by a PG diploma or MA in Public Relations or Corporate Communication.
You are choosing a degree now and want a direct, recognised path with placement support and campus internships built in.

blocks.heading: AI Is Actually Doing to PR Work

items.text: This is not a future risk, it is already showing up in the numbers.

The more useful framing is not "will AI replace PR professionals" but "what changes about what a PR professional actually does." A junior executive today can supervise AI tooling to produce drafts and research that once took two or three people working manually, which raises the bar for what a junior hire is expected to add on top: judgment, accuracy checking, and relationship-building that AI cannot fake.
This makes the entry bar higher, not lower.

blocks.heading: Three Proofs Before You Apply Anywhere

items.text: Before your first real PR application, run yourself through the same three proofs that decide whether anyone is willing to trust you with a real client's story.
Three real tests stand between "interested in PR" and "ready to be hired into PR."
Can you write a real press release and a real media pitch, cold.

blocks.heading: Mistakes That Stall People in PR

items.text: Most of the actual week is writing, research, follow-up emails, and coverage tracking.
A pitch that clearly was not written for the specific journalist gets ignored, and repeat offenders get quietly blacklisted by beat reporters.
A PR professional who can only pitch traditional print and TV media is competing for a shrinking slice of client budgets.

figures.label: PR Industry Market Size
figures.source: PR in India today is not the same job it was a decade ago, and the industry's own data confirms it. According to PRCAI's 2026 SPRINT industry report, India's PR market grew 11% to roughly Rs 3,230 crore in the 2025-26 financial year, and is on track to reach about Rs 4,500 crore by 2030. Inside that growth, the client mix has shifted sharply: government clients now make up around 11% of the top client categories, up from about 4% just a few years ago, and start-ups have expanded their share from roughly 6% to 22% over the same period, while private corporate share has slipped slightly.
